name: Chebe hair ritual
how: A powder of roasted, ground Croton seeds and other plants is mixed with oil or butter, worked along damp, braided lengths, and left in for days.
does: Coats and protects the lengths, so hair breaks less and holds length. It doesn't make hair grow faster from the scalp.
watch: Keep it off the scalp to avoid buildup and itching. Wash out residue regularly, and buy from sellers who list what's in the blend.
modern: Pair with a gentle shampoo on the scalp and low-tension styles. For thinning, minoxidil is the proven option.

name: Alata samina (African black soap)
how: Plant ash from plantain skins and cocoa pods is cooked with shea butter and palm kernel oil into a soft, crumbly soap.
does: A real, effective cleanser. Shea leaves a softer feel than many bar soaps.
watch: Strongly alkaline and can dry the face. Lather in your hands rather than rubbing the bar on skin, since ash bits can scratch.
modern: Follow with a moisturizer. On dry or sensitive faces, keep it for the body.

name: Shea butter (nkuto, ori)
place: West Africa (the shea belt from Senegal to Sudan)
how: Nuts are dried, crushed, roasted and kneaded by hand, mostly by women's cooperatives, then used on skin, hair and babies.
does: An excellent emollient that seals water in. Backed by research on dry skin.
watch: Very rich for acne-prone faces. Refined shea rarely causes nut reactions, but check with a doctor if you have a severe nut allergy.
modern: Use it as the sealing step over a water-based moisturizer. Look for fair-trade or women's co-op shea.

name: Hammam with savon beldi and kessa
how: Steam softens the skin, olive-based black soap is left on for a few minutes, then a rough kessa glove scrubs away dead skin.
does: Leaves skin very smooth for days and is deeply relaxing.
watch: Too often or too hard causes irritation and dark marks, especially on deeper skin tones. Skip the face scrub and freshly shaved skin.
modern: Once a week at most. Follow with body oil or a urea lotion, and never on the same day as an acid.

name: Abhyanga (oil massage)
how: Warm sesame, coconut or herbal oil is massaged over the body, often before a bath.
does: Softens dry skin and relaxes. Coconut oil before washing reduces hair protein loss.
watch: Mustard and some herbal oils can irritate. Oils can clog pores on the face and back.
modern: Keep the ritual. Use lighter oils on the face, and patch test any herbal blend.

name: Ubtan (bridal paste)
how: Gram flour, turmeric, sandalwood and milk or rose water are mixed into a paste and rubbed off the skin before weddings.
does: A gentle exfoliating mask that leaves skin smooth and glowing for the day.
watch: Turmeric stains, and lemon added to some recipes burns in sunlight. Fresh milk spoils, so mix only what you'll use.
modern: Make it fresh each time with water or rose water, skip lemon, and use it as an occasional mask, not a daily scrub.

name: Ssuk (mugwort) baths and steam
how: Dried mugwort is steeped in bath water, burned in moxibustion, or used in steam rooms (jjimjilbang).
does: Warm, calming, and pleasant. Mugwort extract shows soothing effects in K-beauty formulas.
watch: Not during pregnancy; traditionally used to bring on periods. Daisy-family allergy risk.
modern: K-beauty already turned this into standardized extracts. At home, a mugwort bath bag is the safe version.

name: Rice water
place: Japan, China (the Yao women of Huangluo)
how: Water left over from rinsing or fermenting rice is used as a hair rinse and face wash.
does: A pleasant rinse; fermented rice extracts are used in modern formulas. The long-hair legend has little evidence behind it.
watch: Fermented rice water spoils within a day or two and can smell. Left on too long, it can make hair feel stiff.
modern: Make it fresh, rinse it out, and follow with conditioner. Or buy a preserved rice-ferment essence.

name: Gua sha
how: A smooth stone is pressed and stroked across oiled skin, traditionally on the body, now popular on the face.
does: Moves fluid, so the face looks less puffy and more sculpted for a few hours. Feels relaxing.
watch: Facial gua sha should be light. Body-style pressure bruises. Skip active acne and broken skin.
modern: Use a slip of oil or serum and clean the stone after each use. Treat it as a ritual, not a lift.

name: Rose water (gulab, golab)
how: Damask rose petals are steam-distilled; the floral water is splashed or misted on the face and used in pastes.
does: A gentle, refreshing toner that lightly calms skin. Rose extracts show soothing effects in small studies.
watch: Buy rose water made for skin, without added alcohol or fragrance. Unpreserved rose water spoils, so keep it in the fridge.
modern: Use it as a mist before your moisturizer, or as the liquid in clay and herb masks.

name: Sidr hair wash
place: Yemen, Saudi Arabia, and also India and Pakistan
how: Dried leaves of the jujube tree (Ziziphus) are ground and mixed with water into a frothy paste for washing hair and scalp.
does: Natural saponins clean gently and remove buildup while leaving hair soft.
watch: Rinse thoroughly, since leftover powder can itch. Patch test the scalp first.
modern: A good low-foam wash between shampoos, or before henna. For dandruff, a medicated shampoo works better.

name: Henna
place: India, Pakistan, Turkey, Morocco, Sudan, Egypt
how: Crushed henna leaves are mixed into a paste and used for wedding body art and as a hair treatment that coats strands.
does: Coats hair for shine and a reddish tint, and stains skin orange-red to brown for one to three weeks.
watch: Real henna is never black. "Black henna" often contains PPD hair dye, which can cause blistering, scars and a lifelong dye allergy. Henna can make later chemical dyes unpredictable.
modern: Use pure, body-art-quality henna with no metallic salts, and strand test before chemical color or relaxers.

name: Bakhoor (scented smoke)
place: Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Oman, Yemen, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait
how: Wood chips soaked in oud and perfume oils are burned on charcoal, and the smoke is wafted through damp hair and clothing.
does: Leaves a long-lasting signature scent in hair and fabric.
watch: Keep the burner and charcoal well away from hair and loose fabric. Smoke is hard on lungs, so keep sessions short in a ventilated room, and skip it around babies and people with asthma.
modern: For a scented finish without smoke, use a hair perfume or a drop of oud oil diluted in a carrier oil on the lengths only.

name: Kefir masks
how: Women spread fermented milk directly on the face and hair as a mask, then rinsed it away.
does: Mild lactic acid gives a soft glow and smoother feel; on hair, it leaves a soft finish.
watch: Use plain kefir, not flavored or sweetened. Rinse well, and skip it with a dairy allergy. It won't treat acne.
modern: A gentle weekly mask. For breakouts, add a proven active like salicylic acid or adapalene instead.

name: Chamomile tea compresses
how: Chamomile tea is brewed, cooled and dabbed on irritated skin or used as a rinse.
does: Calms irritated skin. A chamomile cream did about as well as weak hydrocortisone in one eczema study.
watch: Tea isn't sterile, so clean cuts with clean water instead. Daisy or ragweed allergy risk.
modern: Make it fresh each time, or use a chamomile (bisabolol) moisturizer for daily calming.

name: Olive oil body care
place: Turkey, Greece, Italy, Lebanon, Palestine, Tunisia
how: Oil is rubbed into skin and hair after bathing, and is the base of traditional soaps like Aleppo and Nabulsi.
does: Softens dry skin and conditions dry hair, especially on damp skin.
watch: Studies found plain olive oil can weaken the skin barrier, so skip it for babies and eczema-prone skin. It can clog pores on the face.
modern: Keep it for body and hair lengths; sunflower or a ceramide cream is better for babies and eczema.

name: Tsubaki (camellia) oil
how: Oil pressed from camellia seeds was combed through hair and smoothed on skin, famously by geisha and kabuki performers.
does: A light, silky oil that smooths frizz and softens dry skin without much greasiness.
watch: Still an oil, so go easy on acne-prone faces. Buy cold-pressed oil sold for skin, not cooking blends.
modern: Use a few drops on damp hair ends or over moisturizer. J-beauty hair oils are often built on it.

name: Nuka-bukuro (rice bran bags)
how: Rice bran was tied in a small cloth bag, soaked in warm bath water and gently rubbed over the face and body.
does: A very gentle cleanse and polish. Rice bran contains ferulic acid and oils that leave skin soft.
watch: Damp bran spoils within a day, so use fresh bran each time. Rinse well.
modern: Japanese enzyme cleansing powders and rice bran washes are the shelf-stable version.

name: Seshin (Korean body scrub)
how: After a long soak, a rough "Italy towel" (ttaemiri) is scrubbed over the whole body until dead skin rolls away.
does: Leaves skin very smooth and feels deeply clean.
watch: It's harsh. Too often or too hard causes rawness and dark marks. Skip it on eczema, sunburn, freshly shaved skin, or while using retinoids or acids.
modern: Once a month at most, after soaking at least 20 minutes, then moisturize right away.

name: Hanbang (Korean herbal skincare)
how: Herbs from traditional Korean medicine, like ginseng, licorice and angelica, were brewed into tonics and washes.
does: The roots of today's luxury K-beauty lines. Ginseng and licorice extracts show antioxidant and calming effects in lab studies.
watch: Strong herbal blends can irritate. Patch test, especially on sensitive skin.
modern: Hanbang creams and essences use standardized extracts. Pair them with sunscreen, which does the heavy lifting against aging.

name: Pearl powder
how: Pearls were ground to a fine powder and dusted on the face or mixed into pastes, linked in legend to Empress Wu Zetian.
does: Mostly a light-reflecting powder that gives a soft glow. Little evidence for whitening or anti-aging claims.
watch: Don't breathe in fine powder. Cheap pearl powders can be contaminated, so buy cosmetic grade from a trusted seller.
modern: Treat it as a setting powder for glow. Use vitamin C or niacinamide for brightening.

name: Thanaka paste
how: Bark from the thanaka tree is ground with water on a stone slab, and the pale yellow paste is painted on cheeks every day.
does: Cooling and fragrant. Lab studies show some antioxidant and mild UV-absorbing effects.
watch: It is not a sunscreen. Use it with an SPF, not instead of one.
modern: Keep the ritual and the look, and wear SPF 30+ underneath for real sun protection.

name: Lulur (Javanese bridal scrub)
how: A paste of rice powder, turmeric, sandalwood and jasmine is rubbed over the body daily before a wedding, then rinsed with yogurt.
does: A gentle body polish that leaves skin smooth and fragrant.
watch: Turmeric stains skin and fabric. Rice-powder scrubs are fine for the body but too rough for the face if rubbed hard.
modern: Make it fresh, use it once or twice a week, and follow with a body moisturizer.

name: Bedak sejuk (cooling rice powder)
how: Rice is fermented, ground and dried into small pellets, often with pandan or jasmine, then mixed with water and dabbed on at night.
does: Cools skin in hot, humid weather and leaves a soft, matte finish.
watch: Fermented rice must be made and dried cleanly, so buy from trusted makers. It can dry out skin with daily use.
modern: Use it on warm nights over a light gel moisturizer, and rinse it off in the morning.

name: Gugo bark shampoo
how: Strips of gugo vine bark are soaked and rubbed in water until they lather, and the foam is used to wash hair.
does: Natural saponins clean the scalp gently and leave hair soft.
watch: Stings the eyes. Patch test the scalp first.
modern: Gugo extract appears in Filipino shampoos, a gentler option for regular washing.

name: Luk pra kob (Thai herbal compress)
how: A cloth ball packed with plai, lemongrass, kaffir lime, turmeric and camphor is steamed and pressed along the body during Thai massage.
does: Warm, aromatic and relaxing. Small Thai studies found it eased knee and muscle pain.
watch: Test the heat on your wrist first, since steamed compresses can burn. Camphor isn't for young children.
modern: Use it for sore muscles, not on the face, broken skin, or during pregnancy without checking first.

name: Bồ kết hair wash
how: Honey locust pods are roasted and boiled, often with lemongrass and grapefruit peel, and the water is used to wash hair.
does: Saponins clean gently, and the herbs leave a fresh scent.
watch: Stings the eyes. Let it cool fully, and patch test.
modern: Vietnamese bồ kết shampoos bottle the same idea in a stable formula.

name: Champi (head oil massage)
how: Coconut, amla or bhringraj oil is massaged into the scalp and hair, often by a mother or grandmother, before washing.
does: Coconut oil before washing reduces protein loss from hair, and the massage is relaxing.
watch: Leaving oil on for days can worsen dandruff. Mustard and herbal oils can irritate, and tight braiding on top pulls at the hairline.
modern: Oil the lengths for an hour or overnight before washing. For dandruff, use a medicated shampoo instead.

name: Ponlei (postpartum turmeric and ginger)
how: After childbirth, mothers are rubbed with turmeric and ginger paste and given warming ginger tea as part of a confinement month of rest and heat.
does: Warm, comforting and part of a rest-first recovery. Turmeric and ginger have anti-inflammatory compounds, though a paste on skin does little beyond warmth and scent.
watch: Ginger and turmeric paste can sting or stain, and should stay off stitches or a C-section wound. Very hot compresses can burn. Check herbal teas with a midwife or doctor while breastfeeding.
modern: Keep the rest, warmth and support. Have postpartum bleeding, fever or wound pain checked by a midwife or doctor.

name: TCM view of skin
how: Skin is read as a sign of inner balance: acne as excess "heat", dullness as stagnant qi and blood, puffiness as "dampness". Care combines herbs, diet, acupuncture and tools like gua sha.
does: Its big idea holds up: sleep, stress, diet and hormones really do show on skin. Some TCM herbs (licorice, green tea, astragalus) have calming or antioxidant effects in lab studies.
watch: Face maps that tie each spot to an organ aren't supported by research; breakouts follow oil, hormones, friction and products. Unregulated herbal creams have been found with steroids. Oral herbs can interact with medicines.
modern: Keep the whole-body view and the gentle tools. Track sleep and stress alongside your skin, and use proven actives for acne or dark marks.

name: Facial cupping
how: Small silicone or glass cups create gentle suction and are glided over oiled skin to move fluid toward the lymph nodes.
does: Temporarily reduces puffiness and feels relaxing, much like gua sha.
watch: Leaving cups in one place leaves bruise-like marks, which are not "toxins". Skip active acne, broken capillaries, rosacea, sunburn and recent filler or Botox.
modern: Keep the cups moving, use a slip of oil, and treat it as a de-puffing massage, a few minutes at a time.

name: Dry brushing
place: Scandinavia, Russia and Ayurveda (garshana with raw silk gloves)
how: A firm natural-bristle brush is swept over dry skin toward the heart before a shower.
does: Exfoliates rough skin on legs and arms and feels invigorating. Any de-puffing is brief.
watch: It doesn't flush "toxins" (the liver and kidneys do that) or remove cellulite. Too hard or too often causes redness, scratches and dark marks. Skip the face, eczema, sunburn and broken skin.
modern: Two or three times a week with light pressure, then moisturize. Skip it on days you use an acid or scrub.

name: Tuscan artisan soap
how: Workshops like Nesti Dante and Saponificio Artigianale Fiorentino make vegetable-oil soaps, often milled and perfumed for gifting. Newer makers such as La Saponaria focus on organic oils, plastic-free packaging and soap sold by the cut.
does: A well-made olive or vegetable soap cleans well and lasts long. Milled bars are harder and longer-lasting; bars sold by the cut skip packaging.
watch: True soap is alkaline (pH around 9 to 10), so even a luxury bar can dry or sting eczema-prone skin and faces. Heavily perfumed gift soaps add fragrance allergens.
modern: Enjoy them on the body. For the face or very dry skin, a fragrance-free syndet bar or gentle cleanser is kinder. Buying unpackaged bars and using a draining soap dish makes them last.

name: Savon de Marseille
how: Olive and other vegetable oils are boiled with soda in large cauldrons over several days, washed, then poured, cut and stamped. Authentic cubes carry at least 72% vegetable oil and are sold unwrapped.
does: A pure, long-lasting, fragrance-free soap that cleans skin, hair, laundry and the house. Plastic-free and biodegradable.
watch: It's still true soap, alkaline at pH 9 to 10, so it can dry very dry skin, eczema and faces. Many "Marseille" bars sold abroad are imitations with fragrance and colour; look for the UPSM mark.
modern: A great plain body and hand soap. Follow with a moisturizer, and use a gentler cleanser on the face. You can make a Marseille-style bar in Make, Soap lye check.

name: Uhie, nzu and uli (Nigerian body art and glow)
place: Nigeria (Igbo, Yoruba, Edo and Hausa traditions)
how: Camwood (uhie or osun) is rubbed on for a warm glow, white nzu clay cools and brightens, uli dye is painted in fine patterns, and tiro (kohl) lines the eyes. Desert date oil gives a body sheen in the north.
does: Beautiful, meaningful body art and a temporary glow. Camwood and clay are gentle on skin for most people.
watch: Traditional tiro is often lead-based galena, so use a cosmetic eyeliner instead. Never eat nzu. Patch test uli and camwood, and keep dyes off broken skin.
modern: Keep camwood and nzu as masks and ceremony paints. For lined eyes, choose a registered eyeliner.

name: La cuarentena (40-day postpartum care)
place: Mexico, Central and South America, the Caribbean
how: For about 40 days after birth, mothers rest, keep warm and are cared for by family. Herbal baths (rosemary, chamomile, marigold), warming teas, abdominal massage (sobada) and wrapping (faja) are common.
does: Rest, warmth, help at home and gentle massage genuinely support recovery and mood. Plantain, calendula and witch hazel washes soothe sore skin.
watch: Rue (ruda) is for baths only and is toxic to drink. Bitter melon (cerasee) and some bitter leaf teas aren't advised while breastfeeding. Wraps shouldn't be tight or used over a fresh C-section without your doctor's okay. Strain herbs well away from stitches.
modern: Keep the rest, warmth and family support. Have bleeding, fever, wound pain and low mood checked by a midwife or doctor.

name: Yadom (Thai herbal inhaler) and phlai oil
how: Menthol, camphor and borneol crystals are blended with dried herbs and packed into a small tube to sniff. Wat Pho's massage school uses compound phlai (Zingiber cassumunar, a ginger relative) oil for aching muscles.
does: The inhaler gives a strong, cooling feeling of an open nose; menthol doesn't actually clear congestion, but it feels like it. Phlai has some anti-inflammatory evidence for sore muscles in small Thai studies.
watch: Inhalers are for sniffing only. Camphor is toxic if swallowed and not for children under 6. "Suitable for eating" on a massage oil is likely a translation slip; don't drink it.
modern: Try the inhaler in Make, Workshop. Use phlai or massage oils on intact skin, away from the face and eyes.

name: Ambunu wash
how: Dried ambunu leaves are steeped in hot water until slippery, strained, and poured over the hair to detangle and wash it, often alongside chebe.
does: The slippery mucilage helps fingers glide through curls, so detangling breaks fewer hairs. It cleans lightly.
watch: Strain well so leaf bits don't knot in hair. Make it fresh each time; plant teas spoil fast.
modern: Use it as a detangling rinse or co-wash. Follow with conditioner if your hair feels dry.

name: Dilka (bridal scrub)
place: Sudan, also Chad and parts of northern Nigeria
how: A dough of sorghum, millet or wheat flour is smoked over fragrant wood, then mixed with oil, mahlab, sandalwood, cloves and khumra perfume. It's rubbed over the body until it rolls off, often in the weeks before a wedding, alongside the dukhan smoke bath.
does: A gentle physical exfoliant: rolling the dough lifts dead skin, so skin feels smooth and looks brighter, and the smoke and perfume leave a lasting scent. It doesn't lighten skin or fade dark spots; any "even tone" is the smoothness and glow from exfoliating.
watch: Smoke the flour outdoors, never in a closed room; wood smoke irritates lungs and the dukhan smoke bath is unsafe in pregnancy and with asthma. Clove oil and strong perfumes can irritate, so patch test. Skip broken, sunburned or freshly shaved skin.
modern: Use it once a week at most, follow with a body oil or lotion, and keep up sunscreen on exposed skin.

name: Khumra (oil perfume)
place: Sudan, also Chad and northern Nigeria
how: A dense perfume oil blended from mahlab (cherry kernel), sandalwood, cloves, musk, amber and other perfumes, warmed over fire and aged, sometimes buried. It's dabbed on warm pulse points, worked into damp skin after dukhan or dilka, and onto braided hair under a scarf.
does: Because it's oil-based and concentrated, the scent sits on skin and hair for a long time, even in dry heat. It's a fragrance, not a skincare treatment.
watch: Traditional blends are very concentrated and can contain clove oil (a strong sensitizer) and synthetic musks, so they can cause rashes or allergy over time. Keep it off the face and broken skin, patch test, and avoid in pregnancy.
modern: Wear it on hair, scarves and clothes, or dilute a drop in a carrier oil for skin. The app has a skin-safe khumra-inspired perfume oil.

name: Luban (frankincense) water
place: Oman, Yemen, Somalia and the Arabian Peninsula
how: A few pieces of food-grade frankincense resin are soaked in water overnight and the water is sipped in the morning. Resin is also chewed like gum and burned as incense in homes and over clothes.
does: Very little of the resin dissolves in water, so the drink is mostly a lightly scented ritual. Concentrated boswellia extracts have some evidence for joint pain, but at doses water can't deliver.
watch: Only food-grade resin; incense resin may be treated or dirty. Skip in pregnancy and check with a doctor if you take blood thinners or anti-inflammatories. Burning incense indoors irritates lungs, so ventilate.
modern: For skin, frankincense essential oil at 1% in a carrier oil is the app's version; see the boswellia body oil recipe.

name: Eat your skincare (Chinese food therapy)
how: Foods are grouped by their effect in Traditional Chinese Medicine. For dryness: snow fungus soup, Asian pear, honey, red dates, peach gum. For puffiness ("dampness"): Job's tears, winter melon, mung bean, chrysanthemum tea, grass jelly. For hair ("kidney and blood"): black sesame, black beans, walnuts, goji, red dates.
does: Many are nourishing, hydrating foods: soups and teas add water, sesame and walnuts add good fats, goji and papaya add vitamins. Cutting salty fried food reduces puffiness. The specific organ claims are traditional ideas rather than tested effects.
watch: Goji can interact with the blood thinner warfarin. Job's tears and some herbal jellies are traditionally avoided in pregnancy. Red dates and dried fruit are high in sugar. Sesame and walnuts are common allergens.
modern: Enjoy them as food alongside a normal routine; for real hair loss or very dry skin, see a doctor.

name: Netra Basti (eye oil bath)
how: A ring of black gram or wheat dough is built around the eyes and filled with warm medicated ghee or oil, which the person blinks through for several minutes.
does: Feels soothing and warm. There's no good evidence it improves eyesight or eye health, though warmth can ease tired, dry-feeling eyes.
watch: Oil pooled on open eyes can carry infection, blur vision and irritate. Never at home with contact lenses, an eye infection, recent eye surgery or any essential oil in the oil.
modern: For screen-tired eyes: preservative-free lubricating drops, regular screen breaks and a warm compress on closed lids. See an eye doctor for ongoing dryness.

name: Sutika Paricharya (Ayurvedic postpartum care)
place: India, Pakistan, Nepal, Sri Lanka and diaspora
how: About 40 days of rest after birth with daily warm oil massage, herbal hair rinses (sage, rosemary, brahmi, ginger), warm baths and warming foods such as gond and almond drinks with jaggery and ginger.
does: Rest, warmth, touch and family support are genuinely good for recovery. The oils and herb rinses comfort and condition; the herbs don't stop normal postpartum hair shedding.
watch: Keep ginger pastes and hot compresses off stitches and C-section wounds. Very hot oil or water burns. Check herbal drinks and supplements with a midwife or doctor while breastfeeding.
modern: Keep the rest and support. Use a plain oil for massage, rinse herbs fresh each time, and have bleeding, fever or low mood checked by a professional.

name: Urli (floating flower bowl)
how: A wide brass or stone bowl by the entrance is filled with water and fresh jasmine, marigold or rose petals, sometimes with floating candles, to scent and welcome.
does: A real, gentle home fragrance with no candle smoke or diffuser. Fresh jasmine buds open through the day and release scent.
watch: Change the water daily: standing water breeds mosquitoes and turns sour within a day or two in heat. Keep it away from pets and toddlers.
modern: Add a few drops of essential oil only to the water, never to skin from the bowl. Compost the flowers when they brown.

name: Shirodhara (warm oil stream)
how: Warm, often herb-infused oil or milk is poured in a steady stream onto the forehead from a hanging pot for 30 to 60 minutes.
does: Deeply relaxing; small studies suggest it eases stress and sleep. Any skin benefit comes from rest and a scalp oil treatment, not a proven 'glow from within'.
watch: Done by a trained therapist with oil at body temperature. Too-hot oil burns; oil in the eyes stings. Wash out with a gentle shampoo, twice if needed.
modern: At home: a warm scalp oil massage (champi) with a plain oil gives much of the same calm.

name: Shashtika Shali / Njavarakizhi (rice bolus massage)
how: Navara rice is cooked in milk and herbal decoction, tied in cloth bundles, and pressed warm over the body, often after an oil massage.
does: Warmth and massage ease muscle tension, and the milky rice leaves skin feeling soft. Claims of nourishing tissue are traditional, not tested.
watch: Bundles must be warm, not hot. Skip on broken skin, rashes or with a dairy allergy.
modern: A warm compress plus a body oil gives a similar relaxing, softening effect at home.

name: Rượu thuốc (herbal rice wine tonics)
how: Dried roots, leaves and mushrooms are steeped in strong rice spirit for weeks to months. The liquid is rubbed into the scalp for hair fall and greys, or onto sore muscles.
does: Alcohol pulls aromatic and bitter compounds out of the herbs, and scalp massage feels good and boosts blood flow while you do it. Arborvitae leaf and ginseng have early studies; most other herbs are traditional only.
watch: Strong spirit dries and stings, so dilute it. Fo-ti is risky taken by mouth; never drink a hair tonic. Dong quai can make skin sun-sensitive.
modern: Vietnamese brands now sell diluted herbal scalp tonics and sprays built on the same herbs.

name: Dehn al oud (oud oil)
place: Arabian Peninsula, with wood from Southeast Asia and India
how: Agarwood darkens and fills with resin when the tree is wounded and infected, its own way of sealing the wound. The resinous wood is soaked and distilled for days into a thick, precious oil, dabbed on skin and beards or burned as chips.
does: Purely scent. Oud is one of the most prized perfume materials in the world, smoky, leathery and long-lasting.
watch: Wild Aquilaria trees are endangered and trade is restricted. Fakes are common. A home tincture of cultivated chips is the realistic DIY.
modern: Most 'oud' in Western perfumes is a synthetic accord; real oud oil can cost more than gold by weight.

name: Bokjumeoni (lucky pouch) and hyangnang (scent sachet)
how: Small silk drawstring pouches, traditionally given at the new year for luck. Scented versions (hyangnang) were filled with dried herbs, flowers or resins and hung from clothing or carried, much like a sachet.
does: Purely scent and ritual. Resins like boswellia (frankincense) and dried roses give a soft, long-lasting smell to a bag or drawer without touching skin.
watch: Keep it dry, since damp herbs go mouldy. Refresh with a drop of essential oil on the resin, not on the fabric, which can stain. Keep away from children and pets who might chew it.
modern: A fabric sachet with frankincense tears, dried rose petals and a few lavender buds, refreshed every month or two.

name: Kibe / tesmi hair butter
how: Fresh butter is washed many times in cold water, then whipped (often with water, herbs such as myrtle, fenugreek, black seed or rosemary, and oils) into a pale, fluffy cream. It's worked into hair and scalp before washing, or in small amounts on braids.
does: Butterfat coats and softens hair, so dry, coily hair feels smoother and breaks less. Claims of faster growth or stopping hair fall haven't been tested.
watch: It's dairy, so it goes rancid and smells, faster with water whipped in. Fine or low-porosity hair can get heavy, limp or stiff. Wash it out within hours, especially in heat.
modern: A whipped shea butter infused with the same dried herbs gives the same softness and keeps for months.
